# SILI ITALICI
<note>Silius Italicus</note>

Amidst this, the consul, ejecting the blood flowing from his lacerated mouth: "Well done, O paternal virtue! Nor are hopes narrow, when such hearts remain for the Romulean kingdom. Take the horse away with spurs, where the wound permits, and from here: let the gates of the city be closed quickly, this pestilence will rush to these walls, say, I pray; let the reins of affairs be handed over to Fabius. My fury fought with our warnings. What more of life remains, except to show the blind plebeians that Paulus knows how to die? Am I carried into the city consumed by wounds? For how much would Hannibal wish to buy it, so that he may see our backs turning? Not such are the hearts to Paulus, nor do we enter the image of the spirits so small. I myself—but why do I delay you, Lentulus, with vain complaint, sick as I am? Proceed and quickly rescue the horse, exhausted by the spear, from here." Then Lentulus seeks the city, carrying great commands; nor does Paulus allow what is left of his light to go unavenged. Just as a tiger, yielding at last to a lethal wound and having thrown its body, struggles with death and opens a languid gap in vain bites, nor being sufficient for its anger with its blows, licks the hunting spears with its final tongue. And now, he had fixed his sword, rising unexpectedly, into the man who was bringing his weapon closer, glittering and secure from the slaughter of Ierta <note>a specific soldier or location</note>, and he was looking around for the Sidonian leader, wishing to place his struggling soul into that right hand. But they conquered the man with weapons gathering from all sides, both the Nomad, and the Garamantian, and the Celt, and the Moor, and the Asturian.

->**Father.**<-

Son, you have spoken rightly. Would to GOD that it were so, for then this art would receive a better name.

->**Son.**<-

But how should I guard myself against such lazy, thieving alchemists? So that they do not persuade me with their great babbling, for you say they are usually great babblers.

->**Father.**<-

I will tell you, my dear son: do not believe them when they come to you and say, "I can bring so much gold surplus into the mark of silver," and "I can bring so much silver into copper with good profit." Likewise: "I can and know a precious <term>augment</term> <gloss>increase/multiplication</gloss>," etc. If you hear such things from them, do not think it is an alchemist; rather, believe me, for I tell you the truth: it is a swindler who intends to bring you out of your possessions with lies. And therefore, go, take a good flail, give it to the artist in his hand, lead him to the barn, and let him practice <term>artes rusticas</term> <gloss>rustic arts/farm work</gloss> there. But if he refuses, then take the flail and use it yourself, and strike the coarse alchemist between the ears with it, so that the red <term>augment</term> drips over his nose. And keep up such work until the <term>Corpus asini</term> <gloss>body of the donkey</gloss> settles down to the earth and remains fixed at the bottom; and such is truly a noble <term>fixation</term> <gloss>stabilizing the volatile substance</gloss>, etc.

Rising from the ground starts with waking at four in the morning. Never lend money without collateral. Not buying what you want is a virtue. It is a loss not to work by the light of the moon. Poverty cannot catch up to those who work. Even if you split a mustard seed into a thousand pieces to burn as wood, you must never throw away the ash. There is nothing that should be discarded. Use the soot from the pot to draw fine eyebrows. A scrap of umbrella paper is a wonderful medicine for numbness. A dry well is a storage place for ladders. Even a rat's tail can be a sheath for an awl. Let the umbrellas dry. Never lend your dried bonito to others. For the pestle, the mortar, the whetstone, the millstone, and the apothecary's mortar—though it is not visible to the eye, there is no case where they do not return diminished every time they are lent. Aside from such things, rely on charm and socializing, but for savings, reading, and the abacus, there is no limit if you look upward. Take those below you as your model. If you follow these rules, even dust will pile up to form a mountain. There is no doubt in these maxims of the wealthy. The Bell of Incessant Hell is but a name; listen to this tale of how fortune and virtue flourish naturally.

### Postscript to the Brief Biography of Zhang Keming

The choice to serve or retire, and one's active achievements, fade like the feeling of leaning on a balcony and looking into a mirror. The winding paths of a cornered foe increase the interest in seeking a valley path. This is the state of mind of the old masters. You are about to seek examination in the Southern Palace; why do you suddenly follow your own path? Yet my heart is delayed here and has not yet been able to fulfill its desires. ### Postscript to the Poems of Monk Nan

In this scroll, Monk Nan asked for my old poems, so I sat and wrote these, along with "Far Travels" and "Autumn Night." Thinking of the mountains and forests, looking up and down at the past and present, I feel deeply moved. Nan's poetry is clear and strict, with ample strength and character. In his leisure, he has absolutely no trace of the "coarseness of a monk." It is like rain that wets apricot blossoms without drenching one's clothes, or a willow wind that blows on the face without being cold. I love it deeply; I do not know what the rest of the world thinks of it. On the last day of the Qingming festival in the <term>Xin-Chou</term> year of <term>Chunxi</term> <gloss>1181</gloss>, written by the Old Man.

# The good inspiration of the angel against vain glory.

<margin>John 15</margin>
<margin>Revelation 4 and 12</margin>
Against the fourth temptation of the devil, the angel gives a good inspiration, saying: "Wretch, why do you boast by ascribing to yourself constancy in faith, hope, and patience (which, however, is to be ascribed only to God), when you have nothing good from yourself?" The Lord says: "Without me you can do nothing." And elsewhere it is written: "Do not arrogate to yourself, do not boast, do not insolently exalt yourself, do not presume anything of yourself, do not attribute anything to yourself." And the Lord says: "Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled." And again: "Unless you become as this little child, you will not enter into the kingdom of heaven." Humble yourself, therefore, and you will be exalted, as the Lord says: "Whoever humbles himself will be exalted." And Augustine says: "If you humble yourself, God will descend to you. If you exalt yourself, God will recede from you." Turn, therefore, your mind away from pride, which once made Lucifer, the most beautiful of angels, the most deformed devil, and cast him from the heights of heaven to the depths of hell, which also was the cause of all sins. Whence Bernard: "Pride is the vanity of every sin and the cause of all perdition." The same: "Remove this vice, and all vices are cut away without labor." Wherefore it is uniquely to be noted that whenever a person dying feels himself tempted by <margin>Isaiah 14</margin> pride, he ought first to consider that pride so displeased God that, on its account alone, He banished the most noble of creatures, Lucifer, with all those adhering to him, from the heavens, damning them eternally. And thus, from such a consideration, he should humble and depress himself by recalling his sins, because he is ignorant of whether he is worthy of hatred or love. Whence he ought especially to take an example from Saint Anthony, to whom the devil said: "O Anthony, you have conquered me, for when I wish to exalt you, you depress yourself; when I wish to depress you, you raise yourself up." Second, he ought to think that humility so pleased God that, on its account, the glorious Virgin Mary conceived God and was exalted above the choirs of angels.

The root of the first two is astringent; for this reason, it is given in a drink with wine to those suffering from diarrhea, in the amount of an astragalus. Its decoction helps with ruptures, spasms, bruises, and chronic cough, and it relieves toothache when used as a mouthwash. The gold-colored one dyes hair and, wherever it is placed, it gathers cockroaches. The leaves, boiled in water, are applied as a poultice for swellings and inflammations of the eyes, and for necrotic sores with honey or wine; with vinegar, it treats wounds and helps those bitten by scorpions. The leaves of the wild one are a poultice for burns, and it is said that the leaves of the female type, when mixed with dried figs, keep them free from rot.

The <term>sighah</term> <gloss>contractual formula</gloss> is an expression indicating the assumption of an obligation towards a right. In its meaning is what was previously discussed under <term>daman</term> <gloss>guaranty</gloss>, such as a person saying: "Zayd has against me" or "with me such-and-such." Excluded by his saying "to Zayd against me or with me" is what he says to him alone without specifying a right, so it is not an acknowledgment unless the acknowledged object is specified, such as "this garment," in which case it is an acknowledgment. 

The expressions "against me" <note>original: "alā"</note> or "in my liability" <note>original: "fī dhimmatī"</note> apply to debt, because that is what is understood from them, and this holds when stated without qualification, not absolute release. Similar to "against me" in admitting clarification <note>original: "taballī al-tafsīr"</note> and in "against me" regarding a <term>wadi'ah</term> <gloss>safekeeping deposit</gloss>, and similar to "against me" in the mother/origin, while "with me" <note>original: "ma'ī"</note> or "at my possession" <note>original: "'indī"</note> are for an identified item; thus if he claims that it was a safekeeping deposit and that it perished, or that it was a pledge, his word is accepted with his oath. My phrasing with "or" in both places is preferable to his phrasing with "and" in both of them.

The reply to "You owe me" or "Is it against you to me?" or "Yes," or "I returned it," or "I acknowledge it," and similar expressions—whether phrased as a denial or an undertaking—constitutes an acknowledgment, because that is what is understood from it. It is like responding to the question "Pay the thousand that you owe me" with "Yes," or with his words "I will lend you," or "Advance me a loan," or "Until I open the purse," or "Until I find the goods," for example, or similar phrases like "Come to take it" or "Wait until you receive it," for indeed that is an acknowledgment of it. 

Conversely, answering that with "Weigh it," or "Take it," or "Judge him," or "Put it into your purse," or "I acknowledge" or "I confess it," and similar expressions, as well as "Valid coins or bad coins," does not constitute an acknowledgment of the thousand, but rather of other than it.

<meta>This page discusses the nature of the human soul after death, challenging Maimonides' view on the "acquired intellect."</meta>

<margin>Therefore</margin>

After it has been explained well that it is impossible to say that the acquired intellect <term>sechel nikneh</term> is what remains after death, it remains for us to explain what is the thing that does remain and how it remains. For it is impossible for anything to remain with a person other than what was within him during life. It is not correct to say that only the material intellect <term>sechel hiyuli</term> remains, because the material intellect is a power within the body, and upon the destruction of the body, it is destroyed (just like hearing and sight). What Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 70 of the first part <note>referring to The Guide for the Perplexed</note>, that the acquired intellect is what remains after death (as we wrote above), is not correct according to the opinion of the philosophers. Therefore, it is impossible to say that the acquired intellect alone remains after death. What appeared correct to say in this matter is that the Divine soul given to man is what remains after death, and it existed before its arrival in the world, and it is eternal, for it is a part of God from above. However, there is a difficulty with this: if so, the soul that remains would be equal in all human beings. ->The matter must be explained well<-

<summary>The author critiques the Maimonidean view that the "acquired intellect" survives death, proposing instead that the eternal Divine soul remains, though noting the complexity of individual differences.</summary>
